note: A point of medieval psychology. The soul has several powers: it feeds the body, it senses, it reasons. When one power is fully taken up, as in deep attention, the others seem to switch off.

The teaching, traced to Plato, that a person has more than one soul, one set above another. Dante follows Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas: there is one soul with several powers. If there were several souls, one could be absorbed while another kept track of the time.

context: Dante has been so absorbed in Manfred's story that he hasn't noticed the morning go by.

note: The sun moves fifteen degrees across the sky each hour, so it rose about three hours and twenty minutes ago. It is mid-morning on Easter Sunday.
The excommunicated of Canto 3, who have been walking with the poets and now point out the way up.

quote: A farmer plugs a greater gap
note: When the grapes ripen, a farmer stops the gaps in his hedge with thorns to keep thieves out. The opening here is smaller than such a gap. It recalls the Gospel saying that the gate to life is narrow and few find it (Matthew 7:14).
A fortress town on top of a sheer rock in the hills of Montefeltro, near San Marino.
A small town on the Ligurian coast, west of Genoa, shut in by cliffs. In Dante's day it was reached from the land by a steep path down.
The Pietra di Bismantova, a great flat-topped rock with sheer sides in the Apennines south of Reggio Emilia. All three are places Dante could have climbed himself.
Legs are not enough here. What carries a soul up this mountain is how much it wants to climb.
Virgil.
Practical advice and a rule for the soul. On this mountain no step should go backward.

quote: a line drawn from mid-quadrant to the center
note: A quadrant is a quarter circle, and also the instrument used to measure angles in the sky. A line from the middle of its arc to the center stands at 45 degrees. The slope is far steeper than that.
They face back the way they came, looking down at the shore and out to the east, where the sun rose.

quote: it struck us from the left
note: In Europe, someone facing east in the morning has the sun on the right, toward the south. Here, south of the equator, the sun passes to the north, on the left. Dante has never seen this.
The north. The sun is passing between the poets and the northern sky.

The twin brothers of Greek myth, who became the constellation Gemini. The sun is in Gemini in early summer, when it climbs farthest north. If it were there now, and not in Aries, Dante would see it even farther to the north.
The sun, which takes its light from God and passes it on. It carries light "up and down", to the northern half of the world and the southern in turn.

The zodiac is the belt of constellations the sun travels through in a year. Dante's Italian word here is rare. Most commentators take it to mean glowing red, the stretch of the zodiac where the sun is. An older reading makes it a toothed wheel.
The Great Bear and the Little Bear, the constellations that circle the north pole of the sky.

The hill of Jerusalem. Jerusalem and Purgatory stand at opposite points of the globe, each at the center of its own hemisphere. The sun's path runs between them, so from Jerusalem it passes to the south and from here to the north.

context: The road he failed to drive is the sun's yearly path through the sky.

note: The celestial equator, the circle in the sky above the earth's equator. The sun is north of it in the northern summer and south of it in the northern winter, so it always lies between the sun and whichever half of the world is having winter.
The people of Jerusalem, who saw the equator to their south, as far off as it lies to the north of Purgatory. Dante says "saw" because the Jews had been scattered from Jerusalem long before his time.
The climb is the cleansing of the soul. The first steps away from sin are the hardest. As each fault is purged the soul grows lighter, until doing good costs no effort at all.
The top of the mountain, where the Garden of Eden is. Virgil's guidance ends there, in Canto 27.

quote: I answer no more than this
note: Virgil says only what reason can know. What lies beyond belongs to Beatrice.

quote: Perhaps you'll need to sit down before then!
note: A dry joke from someone who has been listening. After the long lesson in astronomy, the poem turns to comedy.

quote: standing in the shadow behind the rock
note: The second group of the late repentant: those who put off turning to God out of plain laziness. They lounge here as they lounged in life.
Sloth is one of the seven deadly sins. It is purged on the fourth terrace of the mountain, in Canto 18, where the souls run without rest.
Sarcasm. In Dante's Italian he says "you go on up, since you're so strong". He has just watched Dante arrive out of breath.
He is teasing Dante about the astronomy lesson he has just overheard. He can't be bothered with such questions himself.
Often noted as the first time Dante smiles in the poem. Nothing in Hell allowed it.

context: Dante knows him by his slouch and his few words before he sees his face. The two tease each other like old friends.

note: Dante had feared for his friend's soul. Finding him here means he is saved, however long he must wait.

quote: God's angel sitting at the gate
note: The angel who keeps the gate of Purgatory proper, higher up the slope. Dante reaches it in Canto 9.
The souls want their punishment, because it is the way to Heaven. To be kept from it is the penalty of those who wait here.

context: The lazy must wait outside the gate for as many years as they lived. The excommunicated of Canto 3 wait thirty times the length of their ban.

note: The same rule Manfred gave in Canto 3. Only the prayers of someone living in God's grace are heard.
It is noon in Purgatory, so it is midnight in Jerusalem, on the opposite side of the globe.
For Dante the western edge of the inhabited world, as the Ganges is the eastern. Night now covers that whole half of the globe, from the Ganges to Morocco, where dusk is just falling.
